Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 28, based on the sources I was able to access:

---

## Isaiah 28 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview
Isaiah 28 begins a section (chs. 28–35) directed mainly at Judah, but it opens by addressing the northern kingdom (Ephraim/Israel) first — a rhetorical strategy to confront Judah's sin indirectly before turning the focus directly onto Jerusalem. The chapter features a woe against drunkards, a Messianic cornerstone prophecy, and a closing agricultural parable.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm

---

### vv. 1–4: Woe to the Drunkards of Ephraim

**v. 1:** "Woe to the majestic crown of Ephraim's drunkards…" — The "crown of pride" is Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, built on a hill surrounded by fertile valleys. Ellicott notes the double image: (1) banquet revellers crowned with flower wreaths, and (2) Samaria itself as a fading wreath crowning the "fat valley." The sin condemned is both literal drunkenness and the pride that accompanied Ephraim's prosperity. Gill adds that the Hebrew word for "overcome" (*halam*) means "struck down" or "hammered," picturing wine as something that beats a person into submission.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

**v. 2:** "Behold, the Lord has one who is strong and mighty…" — The "mighty and strong one" is the Assyrian king (Shalmaneser or Sargon), described as God's instrument of judgment. The similitudes of hailstorm, tempest, and flood recall Isaiah 8:7–8 and depict overwhelming, irresistible destruction.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 3:** The "crown of pride" will be trampled underfoot — not merely cast down by hand but trampled, indicating utter destruction and contempt. The repetition of the phrase from v. 1 underscores the certainty of judgment.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 4:** The fading flower "will be like a ripe fig before the summer harvest…" — The early fig (ripening in June) was a special delicacy (Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). Ellicott explains: just as a passer-by eagerly seizes and devours a ripe fig, so the Assyrian king would greedily consume Samaria — a picture of swift, sudden, inevitable destruction. EnduringWord draws a lesson about delayed gratification: the drunkard wants immediate pleasure and consumes it at once, like the fig, with no thought for what follows.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

---

### vv. 5–6: A Crown of Glory for the Remnant

**v. 5:** "On that day the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory…" — In direct contrast to the "crown of pride" of vv. 1–3, the LORD Himself becomes the true crown and diadem for the remnant. Gill notes that Jewish rabbis (cited by Kimchi) expounded this of the King Messiah, and the Targum paraphrases: "In that day shall the Messiah of the Lord of hosts be for a crown of joy." The Pulpit Commentary homiletics sees here the Messianic age when God's own presence replaces faded earthly glory.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 6:** "A spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and a strength to those who repel the onslaught at the gate." — Two blessings for godly governance: wisdom for judges (replacing the corrupt judges of Samaria and Jerusalem) and courage for warriors to drive enemies back to their own city gates. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary sees this fulfilled in Christ granting wisdom and strength to His people.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/isaiah-28.html

---

### vv. 7–8: Drunkenness in Judah

**v. 7:** "These also stagger from wine… priests and prophets reel…" — Isaiah now turns to Judah ("these also"), revealing that the same sin infects the southern kingdom. The threefold repetition of "reel/stagger" emphasises the scandal. Priests were reeling to their services; prophets were reeling in the very act of (false) inspiration. Ellicott notes this violates the prohibition of wine for priests on duty (Lev. 10:1–9). Gill adds that the Hebrew *cohen* can mean "prince" as well as priest, so civil rulers may also be in view.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 8:** "All tables are covered with vomit; there is not a place without filth." — A graphic, almost photographic description of the degradation of drunkenness. EnduringWord (David Guzik, charismatic/Pentecostal) argues that this makes the idea of being "drunk in the Holy Spirit" especially unbiblical — the Spirit is a stimulant who elevates our faculties, not a depressant like alcohol.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

---

### vv. 9–10: The Mocking Response

**v. 9:** "Whom is He trying to teach? … To infants just weaned from milk?" — These are the mocking words of the drunken priests and prophets (vv. 7–8), deriding Isaiah. Ellicott says they ask scornfully: does Isaiah think they are toddlers who need infant-school religion? EnduringWord notes the sarcasm: "Isaiah's message is fit only for children."

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

**v. 10:** "Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there." — The Hebrew consists of monosyllables (*tsav latsav, tsav latsav, qav laqav, qav laqav*). Ellicott says the mockers caricature Isaiah's teaching as wearisome, petty repetition — "always the same old song." However, EnduringWord notes that Isaiah takes the taunt as a compliment: presenting God's word "precept upon precept, line upon line" is exactly the right method. The NIV margin suggests the monosyllables may be meant as meaningless babble — the mockers' imitation of how Isaiah sounded to their alcohol-impregnated minds (Grogan, cited by Guzik).

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

---

### vv. 11–13: Judgment Through Foreign Tongues

**v. 11:** "Indeed, with mocking lips and foreign tongues, He will speak to this people." — Since they rejected plain speech, God will speak through the stammering, barbarous language of Assyrian conquerors. Ellicott notes Paul's application of this verse to the gift of tongues in 1 Corinthians 14:21 — unintelligible speech as a sign of judgment. Gill adds a pastoral interpretation: God first speaks gently as a parent lisping to a child; if that is rejected, He speaks harshly through foreign invaders.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

**v. 12:** God had offered "rest" and "repose," but "they would not listen." — Ellicott says Isaiah is defending himself: far from being a mere repeater of rebukes, he had pointed the way to repentance, rest, and refreshment, but they closed their ears.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 13:** The word of the LORD becomes to them the very "order on order, line on line" they mocked — and the result is that "they will go stumbling backward and will be injured, ensnared, and captured." The preaching that could have led to rest becomes a stumbling stone and a net. Ellicott sees an echo of Isaiah 8:14–15.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

---

### vv. 14–15: The Covenant with Death

**v. 14:** "Therefore hear the word of the LORD, O scoffers who rule this people in Jerusalem." — The focus now narrows specifically to the rulers of Jerusalem. Ellicott identifies these as Hezekiah's chief princes and counsellors — partisans of either an Assyrian or Egyptian alliance rather than the policy of righteousness and repentance.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 15:** "We have made a covenant with death; we have fashioned an agreement with Sheol…" — A proverbial expression (cf. Job 5:23; Hosea 2:18). The scoffers boast that they are safe from the "overwhelming scourge" (a sneer at Isaiah's imagery of the Assyrian invasion as a flood and a scourge). They have made "lies" their refuge and "falsehood" their hiding place. EnduringWord quotes Spurgeon's sermon listing six "refuges of lies": the lie that we are good enough, the lie of fatalism, confidence in new false teachings, mere religious profession, having a saved soul with an unchanged life, and trusting an old experience instead of an ongoing relationship.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

---

### vv. 16–17: The Precious Cornerstone

**v. 16:** "See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken." — This is one of the most important Messianic prophecies in Isaiah, quoted in the New Testament at Romans 9:33, 10:11; Ephesians 2:20; and 1 Peter 2:6. The image is of an enormous foundation stone, tested and proven, by which the whole building is aligned. Ellicott notes the "tried stone" (literally "stone of proof") may mean one that stands every test or one that tests those who come in contact with it, becoming either a sanctuary or a "stone of stumbling" (cf. Luke 2:34–35; 20:18). The phrase "will never be shaken" (or "shall not make haste") contrasts the calm of faith with the panic of unbelief. The LXX renders it "shall not be ashamed," followed by Paul in Romans 9:33.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/28-16.html

*On differing interpretations:* The StudyLight.org compilation of commentaries notes that while all orthodox traditions see Christ here, some older commentators (Rawlinson) thought "Jehovah himself would seem to be the Rock." The Targum renders it "Lo! I appoint in Zion a king, a strong, mighty, and terrible king." Prof. Driver suggested that the prophecy had an immediate reference to present security (God's presence and temple in Zion) but that a Messianic reference is genuinely included. The Pulpit Commentary raises the question of whether Isaiah himself understood it as Messianic or whether he simply meant that God had set His name in Jerusalem.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/28-16.html

**v. 17:** "I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level…" — The architectural imagery continues: God not only lays the cornerstone but keeps the building straight with justice and righteousness. The "hail" and "water" will sweep away the false refuge of lies. This contrasts the true foundation in Christ with the flimsy shelter of falsehood.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

---

### vv. 18–19: The Covenant with Death Annulled

**v. 18:** "Your covenant with death will be dissolved… When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it." — The very scourge the scoffers boasted would not touch them will trample them. Their treaty with death is worthless.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

**v. 19:** The scourge passes "morning after morning, by day and by night," and "the understanding of this message will bring sheer terror." — Ellicott notes the word for "report" (or "message") is the same as the "doctrine" of v. 9 — the very message they mocked. Now understanding it brings only terror, not rest.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

---

### v. 20: The Bed Too Short and Blanket Too Narrow

**v. 20:** "Indeed, the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you." — This is the subject of a full sermon by C.H. Spurgeon (Baptist, 1859). He interprets the bed and covering spiritually: the soul needs rest (sleep) and covering (clothing). The world's beds — riches, fame, pleasure — are all too short; human desire always exceeds them. Only Christ provides a bed long enough for the soul to stretch out upon and a covering broad enough to wrap around the largest sinner. Ellicott applies it historically: Hezekiah's counsellors had "made their bed" in the Egyptian alliance, but it would prove altogether inadequate.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-28.html
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

---

### v. 21: The LORD's "Strange Work"

**v. 21:** "For the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim… to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task." — At Mount Perazim (2 Sam. 5:20) and the Valley of Gibeon (Josh. 10:11; 1 Chron. 14:16), the LORD fought *for* Israel against her enemies. Now He will rise up *against* His own people — this is His "strange" or "awesome" work because it is contrary to His usual pattern of defending Israel. Ellicott calls it "the very paradox of prophecy."

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

---

### v. 22: A Decree of Destruction

**v. 22:** "So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier. Indeed, I have heard from the Lord GOD of Hosts a decree of destruction against the whole land." — Ellicott notes that mocking will only tighten the fetters already binding them. The "decree of destruction" echoes Isaiah 10:23, probably singled out by the scoffers for derision.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

---

### vv. 23–29: The Parable of the Farmer

**v. 23:** "Listen and hear my voice. Pay attention and hear what I say." — The opening formula resembles the style of the Wisdom books (Proverbs 2:1; 4:1; Psalm 34:11). Isaiah is about to deliver a parable without giving the interpretation, challenging the hearers to discern.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 24:** "Does the plowman plow for planting every day? Does he continuously loosen and harrow the soil?" — Ploughing represents preparatory discipline (cf. Jer. 4:3). It is a means, not an end, and therefore only for a season. Ellicott sees this as hope: the Assyrian "ploughing" of the land is preparing the way for a better harvest.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 25:** The farmer sows different seeds by different methods — caraway (or fennel) and cumin are scattered broadcast; wheat, barley, and rye are planted in rows. Ellicott identifies each verb as carefully chosen for the specific agricultural process. The point: the wise farmer is discriminating in his methods, dealing with each seed according to its nature. So it is with the great Husbandman whose field is the world.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 26:** "For his God instructs and teaches him properly." — The farmer's skill, seemingly the outcome of long experience, is actually a gift from God. Ellicott compares the pagan myths of Osiris, Triptolemus, and Dionysus as gods of agriculture; Isaiah states the fact without the myth.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 27:** "Surely caraway is not threshed with a sledge… caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod." — Different crops require different threshing methods. The small, delicate seeds (caraway/fennel, cumin) are gently beaten with a light rod or stick, not crushed under a heavy threshing sledge or cartwheel. Ellicott interprets: God deals gently with the "little ones of the earth" — tribulation comes in measure and season.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 28:** "Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed…" — Bread corn (wheat, barley) undergoes severer threshing, but even this is not endless. The end of threshing is preservation, not destruction — to separate the precious from the worthless. The wheels stop when their work is done.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm

**v. 29:** "This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom." — The climax uses the highest Divine name ("LORD of Hosts") rather than the simpler "God" (Elohim) of v. 26. The farmer's wisdom is a parable of God's own government: varied, discriminating, purposeful, and always aimed at a good harvest. EnduringWord notes that the farmer doesn't only plow; he knows when to stop and when to plant — and so God knows the right timing and measure of judgment and grace.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/28.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-28/

---

## Summary of Differing Interpretations

**v. 10 — "Order on order, line on line":**
- Traditional (Ellicott, Gill): the drunkards' mocking imitation of Isaiah's preaching. Isaiah then reclaims the phrase as the right method of teaching.
- EnduringWord (Pentecostal/charismatic): adds that this implies God teaches us "by degrees" — a little at a time.
- Some modern commentators (Wolf, Grogan, cited by Guzik): the Hebrew monosyllables may be deliberately meaningless — mimicking how Isaiah sounded to intoxicated ears.

**v. 16 — The Cornerstone:**
- All Protestant traditions see Christ here (1 Pet. 2:6; Eph. 2:20; Rom. 9:33).
- The Targum (Jewish) renders it: "Lo! I appoint in Zion a king."
- Pulpit Commentary raises the question whether Isaiah himself understood it as Messianic or meant it as God's presence in Zion being the true security (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/28-16.html).
- The NET Bible and modern scholarship (Driver, cited on biblehub.com) suggest an immediate historical reference (God's presence/temple) with a genuine but secondary Messianic dimension.
- Calvin (cited on StudyLight): "This fruit of faith is elsewhere described by Paul, when he says 'being justified by faith, we obtain peace with God.' The Apostles show that this 'stone' is Christ."

**v. 8 — "Drunk in the Holy Spirit":**
- EnduringWord (David Guzik, charismatic tradition) explicitly rejects the notion of being "drunk in the Holy Spirit" as unbiblical, arguing alcohol is a depressant while the Holy Spirit is a stimulant that elevates all our faculties. This is a point of tension within Pentecostal/charismatic circles.

**v. 20 — The Short Bed:**
- Spurgeon (Baptist) applies it entirely spiritually: the soul's search for rest and covering, finding both only in Christ.
- Ellicott applies it historically to Hezekiah's inadequate Egyptian alliance.
